Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or SHA1 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or MD5 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or SHA1 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or MD5 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["87603ea025623b19954e460add532048"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ARToken: Inside an EvilTokens affiliate panel targeting Microsoft 365

Cisco Talos
2026-07-01 16 use cases 12 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Talos has identified "ARToken," a phishing-as-a-service platform that targets Microsoft 365. The ARToken panel exposes 80+ API endpoints for device code phishing, Primary Refresh Token persistence, email access, BEC operations, and SharePoint exfiltration.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ARToken vendor-impersonation phish: inbound mail failing SPF+DKIM+DMARC with pumber.png signature lure · [LLM] SharePoint tenant lookalike via .com-folding (mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com) in phishing URL · [LLM] ARToken Cloudflare Workers lure delivery: {uuid}-docviewer/onedrive/adobe2/document.workers.dev · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] EvilTokens device-code phishing API call: POST /api/device/start with clientMode broker to C2 · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] EvilTokens PRT persistence chain: /prt/setup /prt/refresh /prt/renew /prt/reacquire /prt/cookie to C2 · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint egress to ARToken C2 / phishing infrastructure (pamconj.com, workers.dev) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ARToken vendor-impersonation phish: inbound mail failing SPF+DKIM+DMARC with pumber.png signature lure AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the ARToken initial-access email that spoofs a trusted vendor's accounts-payable contact: inbound, delivered, all three sender-auth checks (SPF, DKIM body-hash, DMARC compauth=none) failing, carrying the outstanding-invoice lure. Anchored on the article's inline signature attachment pumber.png to raise fidelity above generic auth-fail noise. Rationale: Combines the article's stated triple auth-failure (compauth=none reason=405) with the concrete inline signature attachment pumber.png and the outstanding-invoice lure theme — far higher fidelity than auth-fail alone. Reply-To vs From pivot noted by Talos is not a first-class column in the mail-security schemas, so pumber.png + full auth failure is the durable anchor.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656 T1036.005
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor whose mail server misconfigures SPF/DKIM and coincidentally attaches an image named pumber.png (extremely unlikely)
  • Marketing/newsletter senders from mis-delegated subdomains failing all three checks
  • Forwarded internal mail losing DKIM alignment
  • A genuine AP invoice thread where the vendor's DMARC broke after a DNS change
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("yourtrusteddomain.com") // maintain an allowlist of vendor domains that legitimately fail alignment post-DNS-change
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the message, confirm SenderFromAddress domain is a known vendor while SenderMailFromAddress/sending IP is unrelated, and check the Reply-To header for an off-domain redirect. 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete via EmailPostDeliveryEvents, block the Reply-To domain, and warn the recipient AP mailbox. 3) Hunt: search for other recipients of the same pumber.png attachment or the same sending IP, and pivot any embedded *.sharepoint.com anchor into UC 'SharePoint tenant lookalike'.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| extend AD = parse_json(AuthenticationDetails)
| where tostring(AD.SPF) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DKIM) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DMARC) =~ "fail"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "pumber.png"
    | project NetworkMessageId, SigImage = FileName
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, SigImage, SenderIPv4, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents

  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, SigImage, SenderIPv4, NetworkMessageId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint tenant lookalike via .com-folding (mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com) in phishing URL AIDelivery High
Detects the ARToken redirect trick where the visible anchor shows the vendor's real tenant (mononapfp.sharepoint.com) but the href targets an attacker tenant that folds the vendor's '.com' into the tenant label (mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com), inheriting SharePoint's clean reputation. Flags the concrete IOC plus the generic tenant-name-ending-in-'com' folding pattern. Rationale: Uses the exact attacker tenant mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com from the article plus the generalised '.com-folding' regex (tenant label ending in 'com' before .sharepoint.com) that captures the evasion class. Because the destination is still a real sharepoint.com host, reputation-based controls miss it — the tenant-label anomaly is the only reliable signal.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate company whose tenant name genuinely ends in 'com' (e.g. brand called 'Xcom' → xcom.sharepoint.com)
  • Internal users legitimately collaborating with a partner tenant that happens to match the pattern
  • Security-team detonation/sandbox traffic to the lookalike during investigation
  • Safe Links rewrite pre-fetch resolving the domain without a real user click
Suppression filter
| where Name !in~ ("xcom.sharepoint.com") // allowlist known-legit tenants whose label ends in 'com'
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the recipient(s), confirm the tenant label is not a real customer tenant (compare against your SharePoint external-sharing partner list), and pull the source email/anchor text. 2) Contain: block *com.sharepoint.com lookalikes at the proxy/URL filter for the specific tenant, revoke any Safe Links click-through, and force sign-out for users who clicked. 3) Hunt: correlate the resolving hosts to device-code auth (UC3) and any subsequent AAD sign-in from a new IP/device within 30 minutes.
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where UrlDomain endswith ".sharepoint.com"
| where UrlDomain =~ "mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com" or UrlDomain matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com$"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith ".sharepoint.com"
| where Name =~ "mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com" or Name matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens device-code phishing API call: POST /api/device/start with clientMode broker to C2 AIExploitation High
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens device-code phishing exchange on web-proxy telemetry: a POST to /api/device/start against attacker C2 (spx.pamconj.com) carrying the non-standard clientMode:"broker" body used to drive Microsoft's WAM broker flow for MFA-bypass token capture. This is the credential-access request that precedes victim token theft. Rationale: The article documents the exact API contract (POST /api/device/start, clientMode:"broker") matching the Sekoia-documented EvilTokens C2, and names spx.pamconj.com as the C2 host. Path + host together are high-fidelity and platform-specific to this kit. Detection lives on proxy/SWG telemetry (Defender endpoint cannot see the URL path), so defender_kql is intentionally empty; endpoint DNS to the same host is covered by the C2-egress UC.
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002 T1078.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal app that coincidentally exposes an /api/device/start route on a non-pamconj host (excluded by the host filter)
  • Security research/detonation of the kit from a sanctioned sandbox
  • Proxy log replay/testing
  • URL-scanner pre-fetch of the endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify SrcUsername/SrcIpAddr, confirm the destination is attacker-controlled (spx.pamconj.com / *pamconj.com), and check the user's AAD SigninLogs for a device-code (deviceCode) authentication within minutes. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken / conditional-access session revoke), disable the account if a token was issued, and block *.pamconj.com. 3) Hunt: pivot to the PRT-lifecycle UC for /prt/* calls from the same host and to any new device registration on the account.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/api/device/start"
| where DstHostname has "pamconj.com" or Url has "pamconj.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, DstHostname, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens PRT persistence chain: /prt/setup /prt/refresh /prt/renew /prt/reacquire /prt/cookie to C2 AIInstallation High
Hunts the Primary Refresh Token persistence lifecycle that Sekoia flagged as EvilTokens' core differentiator, reproduced in ARToken: web requests to /prt/setup, /prt/refresh, /prt/renew, /prt/reacquire and /prt/cookie against the pamconj.com C2. These calls maintain persistent, MFA-immune access to a compromised Microsoft 365 identity. Rationale: Uses the five named PRT endpoints and the pamconj.com C2 host from the article — the exact persistence chain Sekoia documented for EvilTokens. Requiring the pamconj.com host alongside /prt/* removes any chance of colliding with legitimate internal token services. Path-level signal is proxy-only, so defender_kql is empty by design.
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal identity-service using a /prt/ path on a non-pamconj host (excluded by host filter)
  • Sanctioned red-team emulating EvilTokens PRT flows
  • Proxy log testing/replay
  • Reverse-proxy health checks hitting a /prt/ route on unrelated infrastructure
Response runbook
1) Triage: map SrcUsername to an AAD identity, confirm the C2 host, and review AAD AuditLogs for a 'Register device'/'Add registered owner' event and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs refresh-token reuse for that user. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens, delete any attacker-registered device object, disable the account, and block *.pamconj.com. 3) Hunt: enumerate mailbox inbox-rule creation (forwarding/hiding) and SharePoint file access for the account, and search for other users hitting the same /prt/* C2.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname has "pamconj.com" or Url has "pamconj.com"
| where Url has_any ("/prt/setup","/prt/refresh","/prt/renew","/prt/reacquire","/prt/cookie")
| summarize DistinctPrtEndpoints = dcount(Url), Endpoints = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname
| order by LastSeen desc

ARToken Cloudflare Workers lure delivery: {uuid}-docviewer/onedrive/adobe2/document.workers.dev AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoint navigation/DNS to the ARToken phishing lure domains served from Cloudflare Workers with the kit's UUID-prefixed themed subdomains (docviewer, onedrive, adobe2, document). These pages host the seven-layer client-side anti-bot gate before delivering the device-code capture flow. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named Cloudflare Workers lure patterns ({uuid}-docviewer/-onedrive/-adobe2.workers.dev) plus the concrete IOC clear90489058903-document.workers.dev. The UUID-prefixed themed subdomain is the kit's fingerprint; the seven-layer anti-bot logic itself lives in the served JS (not in standard logs), so we detect the delivery domain that hosts it.
ATT&CKT1102 T1497 T1027
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers/QA hitting their own *.workers.dev deployments whose subdomain coincidentally contains 'document' or 'onedrive'
  • SaaS products that host document viewers on Cloudflare Workers
  • Security sandbox detonation of the lure
  • URL-scanner/Safe-Links pre-fetch resolving the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-dev") // exclude known developer/CI accounts that deploy to workers.dev
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user, confirm the workers.dev subdomain matches the UUID-prefix + theme fingerprint, and check whether a device-code auth or *.sharepoint.com lookalike followed on the same host. 2) Contain: block the specific workers.dev FQDN (and add a watch for the {uuid}-theme pattern), and warn the user; revoke tokens if auth followed. 3) Hunt: baseline all first-seen *.workers.dev resolutions org-wide (leftanti against 30-day baseline) and correlate to the pamconj.com C2 UCs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)[a-f0-9-]+-(docviewer|onedrive|adobe2|document)\.workers\.dev" or RemoteUrl has "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name matches regex @"(?i)[a-f0-9-]+-(docviewer|onedrive|adobe2|document)\.workers\.dev" or Name =~ "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint egress to ARToken C2 / phishing infrastructure (pamconj.com, workers.dev) AICommand & Control High
Domain-level net for any host resolving or connecting to ARToken command-and-control infrastructure: the pamconj.com family (pamconj.com, dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com) and the known Cloudflare Workers lure clear90489058903-document.workers.dev. This is the catch-all C2/exfil indicator across DNS and network telemetry. Rationale: Uses the article's pre-extracted C2 IOCs verbatim (pamconj.com, dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev). Fixed the prior validation error by pivoting Sentinel to DnsEvents.Name (a real column) instead of the nonexistent DnsEvents.IPAddresses. Named-domain contact is directly attributable and low-FP.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst or sandbox intentionally resolving the C2 during investigation
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment/validation tooling touching the IOCs
  • Passive-DNS or scanner appliances resolving the domain
  • Sinkholed domain (post-takedown) resolving to a benign park IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" // exclude security tooling and machine-account enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) that made the request and confirm it isn't a sanctioned TI/sandbox tool. 2) Contain: isolate the host if a user browser/Office process initiated it, block *.pamconj.com and the workers.dev FQDN at DNS/proxy, and revoke tokens for any associated user. 3) Hunt: pivot to the device-code (/api/device/start) and PRT (/prt/*) UCs for the same host/user, and sweep the org for other resolvers of pamconj.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "pamconj.com" or RemoteUrl has "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith "pamconj.com" or Name =~ "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP + companion APK by SHA256 on endpoints · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Montana Empire kit PHP components staged on web infrastructure · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AI coding-assistant egress to first-seen external domain (phantom squatting) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP + companion APK by SHA256 on endpoints AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the two Unit 42-published Montana Empire artifacts landing on managed endpoints: the 7,958,528-byte kit ZIP (postal-service brand clone with PHP backend + Telegram C2) and the 12,649,472-byte malicious 'post' APK. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact file hashes rather than any generic phishing behaviour. Rationale: Uses the two SHA256 hashes Unit 42 published for the Montana Empire kit ZIP (7,958,528 bytes) and companion [redacted]post.apk (12,649,472 bytes); both hashes were independently confirmed on the origin-unit42 mirror and CyberPress write-up, so they meet the two-source bar. Cross-checked against: • https://origin-unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://cyberpress.org/ai-hallucinated-domain-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/phantom-squatting-uses-ai-hallucinated.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or threat-intel researcher intentionally downloading the sample to a sandbox VM
  • Security team seeding the hash into a detonation/AV-test host
  • Incident-response evidence collection copying the artifact to a forensic share
  • EDR retro-scan re-surfacing a quarantined copy already handled

Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256, the landing path, and the InitiatingProcess/User that wrote or ran it; verify the host is not a known malware-analysis sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, quarantine/delete the ZIP and APK, and block both hashes org-wide via custom IOC. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing process and user to any browser/email download source, look for the kit's PHP files (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php) or Telegram (api.telegram.org) egress, and check whether the APK was forwarded to other users.

Montana Empire kit PHP components staged on web infrastructure AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the Montana Empire kit's distinctive server-side PHP files (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php) being written to disk or requested over HTTP, indicating the postal-service phishing clone is being staged or is live on infrastructure you can see. Article-specific because these three filenames are the kit's internal component names, not generic web paths. Rationale: Pivots on the three exact PHP component names Unit 42/CyberPress attribute to the Montana Empire kit (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php); these are non-generic internal filenames, so a file-create or IIS request for them is high-fidelity for kit staging on visible infra. Cross-checked against: • https://origin-unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://cyberpress.org/ai-hallucinated-domain-theft/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named panel_track.php in an unrelated in-house web app
  • Pen-test / red-team dropping a lookalike phishing kit during an authorised exercise
  • WAF or scanner replaying kit URIs against your site (request hits with 404s, no file on disk)
  • Security researcher unpacking the kit ZIP on an analysis host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the hit is a file-write (kit staged locally) vs an inbound IIS request (external probing); check the folder path, writing process, and HTTP status. 2) Contain: if written to your web root, take the site offline / remove the files and preserve a forensic copy; if inbound-only, block the source IP and confirm no 200 responses. 3) Hunt: look for the kit ZIP hash on the same host, outbound connections to api.telegram.org (kit C2), and any web-shell-style process (php/w3wp spawning cmd/powershell).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("panel_track.php","verify_api.php","mentalite.php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("panel_track.php","verify_api.php","mentalite.php")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding-assistant egress to first-seen external domain (phantom squatting) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the article's core TTP: an AI coding assistant / agent process (Cursor, VS Code+Copilot, Windsurf, Ollama, etc.) making an outbound connection or DNS query to an external domain the org has never seen before — the moment an LLM-hallucinated, adversary-pre-registered 'phantom' domain is fetched with zero reputation. Article-specific because it scopes rare-domain egress to AI-assistant parent processes, the exact trust surface Unit 42 describes. Rationale: No hard domain IOC exists (Unit 42 redacted the live phantom domains and the build-notifier[.]io URL is explicitly illustrative), so this targets the behavioural core of the article — an AI dev-assistant binary reaching a zero-reputation, never-before-seen external domain — via a 30-day leftanti baseline scoped to named AI-client processes. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/phantom-squatting-uses-ai-hallucinated.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately adopting a new SaaS/API the AI assistant correctly recommended (real, newly-used domain)
  • AI extension auto-update or telemetry endpoint not yet in baseline
  • First use of a new package registry mirror or docs CDN
  • Newly onboarded host with no 30-day baseline generating many first-seen domains
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".github.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".githubcopilot.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".openai.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".anthropic.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".ollama.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".visualstudio.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the first-seen domain's registration age (WHOIS) and reputation; a domain registered within days that matches a brand's naming pattern is the phantom-squat signal, whereas an established SaaS domain is benign. 2) Contain: if the domain is newly-registered/unreputed, block it at DNS/proxy and warn the developer not to hardcode the URL; capture what data the assistant sent. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same domain, check whether the URL was committed into source/config, and review the AI-assistant session for other hallucinated endpoints.
let AiClients = dynamic(["cursor.exe","code.exe","windsurf.exe","ollama.exe","copilot.exe","continue.exe","claude.exe"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AiClients)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;

| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and RemoteIPType == "Public"

| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 5) by RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fission Environment CRD create/update with dangerous SecurityContext on standalone container (CVE-2026-50566) AIExploitation High
Hunts Kubernetes API audit events where a Fission Environment CRD (apiGroup fission.io) is created/updated carrying privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous-capability SecurityContext specifically on the standalone spec.runtime.container / spec.builder.container fields — the exact field the round-4 PodSpec sanitiser missed. This is the earliest and highest-fidelity catch of the CVE-2026-50566 admission bypass before any pod is scheduled. Rationale: Pivots on the exact article strings: objectRef.resource=environments + apiGroup fission.io, and the standalone spec.runtime.container/spec.builder.container securityContext fields with privileged/allowPrivilegeEscalation/SYS_ADMIN/NET_ADMIN/SYS_PTRACE — the precise merge-layer gap named in the advisory PoC. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty because K8s API audit telemetry is not in those schemas. Corroborated against NVD and GitLab/CIRCL advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m63v-2g9w-2w6v • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50566 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/fission/fission/CVE-2026-50566/
ATT&CKT1611 T1610 T1548
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cluster administrator deliberately creating a debug/system Fission Environment with elevated capabilities (should be rare and reviewed)
  • GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux) reconciling an Environment manifest that legitimately declares NET_ADMIN for a networking function
  • Fission upgrade/CI tooling re-applying pre-existing environment definitions
  • Security team re-running the CVE-2026-50566 PoC during patch validation
  • A pre-existing (pre-patch) privileged environment being updated for an unrelated field, re-emitting the SecurityContext
Suppression filter
| where Actor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and Actor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:" and Actor !endswith ":cluster-admin"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the Username/service account and sourceIPs on the audit event; confirm it is a tenant (not cluster-admin) principal and check whether the Environment name/namespace is expected. Verify cluster Fission version < 1.24.0 (vulnerable). 2) CONTAIN: Delete or revert the offending Environment CRD; revoke environments.fission.io create/update RBAC from the identity; apply a Kyverno/OPA policy rejecting dangerous container SecurityContext and label the function/builder namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all pods in fission function/builder namespaces for privileged/added-capability containers (UC2); review audit logs from the same principal for exec/attach into resulting pods, node filesystem access, and secret reads indicating a completed escape.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "environments" and tostring(ObjectRef.apiGroup) == "fission.io"
| extend RuntimeSC = RequestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext
| extend BuilderSC = RequestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext
| where tostring(RuntimeSC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(BuilderSC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(RuntimeSC.allowPrivilegeEscalation) == "true"
    or tostring(BuilderSC.allowPrivilegeEscalation) == "true"
    or tostring(RuntimeSC.capabilities.add) has_any ("SYS_ADMIN","NET_ADMIN","SYS_PTRACE")
    or tostring(BuilderSC.capabilities.add) has_any ("SYS_ADMIN","NET_ADMIN","SYS_PTRACE")
| project TimeGenerated, Verb, Actor = Username, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), EnvName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), RuntimeSC, BuilderSC, UserAgent, SourceIPs = RequestObject.spec
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fission Environment CRD Privileged Standalone Container SecurityContext (CVE-2026-50566)
id: 6f3b1c8a-2d4e-4a91-9b7c-8e1a2f5c9d20
description: Detects create/update of a Fission Environment CRD whose standalone runtime.container or builder.container SecurityContext requests privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous Linux capabilities, bypassing the PodSpec-only admission validation.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m63v-2g9w-2w6v
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50566
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1611
  - attack.t1610
  - attack.t1548
logsource:
  product: kubernetes
  service: audit
detection:
  selection_resource:
    verb:
      - create
      - update
      - patch
    objectRef.resource: environments
    objectRef.apiGroup: fission.io
  selection_priv:
    requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.privileged: true
  selection_bpriv:
    requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.privileged: true
  selection_ape:
    requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: true
  selection_bape:
    requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: true
  selection_caps:
    requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.capabilities.add|contains:
      - SYS_ADMIN
      - NET_ADMIN
      - SYS_PTRACE
  selection_bcaps:
    requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.capabilities.add|contains:
      - SYS_ADMIN
      - NET_ADMIN
      - SYS_PTRACE
  condition: selection_resource and (selection_priv or selection_bpriv or selection_ape or selection_bape or selection_caps or selection_bcaps)
level: high
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:environments @objectRef.apiGroup:fission.io (@requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation:true OR @requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation:true OR @requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.capabilities.add:(SYS_ADMIN OR NET_ADMIN OR SYS_PTRACE) OR @requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.capabilities.add:(SYS_ADMIN OR NET_ADMIN OR SYS_PTRACE))
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" (verb=create OR verb=update OR verb=patch) objectRef.resource=environments objectRef.apiGroup=fission.io
| spath output=priv path=requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.privileged
| spath output=bpriv path=requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.privileged
| spath output=ape path=requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
| spath output=bape path=requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
| spath output=caps path=requestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext.capabilities.add{}
| spath output=bcaps path=requestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext.capabilities.add{}
| where priv="true" OR bpriv="true" OR ape="true" OR bape="true" OR match(caps,"SYS_ADMIN|NET_ADMIN|SYS_PTRACE") OR match(bcaps,"SYS_ADMIN|NET_ADMIN|SYS_PTRACE")
| table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name priv bpriv ape bape caps bcaps sourceIPs{}
| sort - _time
Privileged / dangerous-capability pod scheduled in Fission function/builder namespace by executor SA AIInstallation Medium
Defence-in-depth for CVE-2026-50566: catches the resulting pod when the Fission executor/buildermgr service account schedules a pod containing a privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous-capability container. Fires even if a future variant uses a different bypass field, because it inspects the actual materialised Pod SecurityContext rather than the Environment CRD. Rationale: Targets the materialised outcome described in the impact section: a privileged/dangerous-capability container scheduled under the executor's high-privilege service account (system:serviceaccount:fission*) or bearing the fission environmentName label. Complements UC1 by inspecting the Pod SecurityContext directly, so it survives field-name variants of the bypass. K8s-audit-only telemetry, hence Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m63v-2g9w-2w6v • https://www.thehackerwire.com/fission-critical-container-escape-and-privilege-escalation-cve-2026-50566/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately privileged Fission system component if the operator intentionally runs one (verify against Fission Helm values)
  • Node-level DaemonSets sharing the fission namespace that legitimately require NET_ADMIN
  • Third-party admission mutating webhook injecting a privileged sidecar into fission pods
  • Migration/upgrade jobs run by the fission executor SA during a version bump
  • Cluster monitoring agent pod co-scheduled in the fission namespace with SYS_PTRACE for profiling
Suppression filter
| where ContainerName !in ("fission-fetcher") and PodGenerateName !startswith "fission-upgrade"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the pod's ownerReference/environmentName label ties it to a Fission Environment, and cross-reference UC1 to see which Environment CRD produced it; note the executor SA and namespace. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the pod and its parent Environment/Deployment; cordon the node it landed on and inspect for host mount or hostPID/hostNetwork abuse; rotate any secrets reachable from that namespace. 3) HUNT: kubectl-audit for exec/attach into the pod, and check node auditd/EDR for container-escape indicators (writes to /proc, host filesystem access, nsenter). Sweep all fission namespaces for other privileged pods and enumerate identities holding environments.fission.io create/update RBAC.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb == "create" and tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "pods"
| where Username startswith "system:serviceaccount:fission" or isnotempty(tostring(RequestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName))
| mv-expand Container = RequestObject.spec.containers
| extend SC = Container.securityContext
| where tostring(SC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(SC.allowPrivilegeEscalation) == "true"
    or tostring(SC.capabilities.add) has_any ("SYS_ADMIN","NET_ADMIN","SYS_PTRACE")
| project TimeGenerated, ExecutorSA = Username, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), PodGenerateName = tostring(RequestObject.metadata.generateName), EnvLabel = tostring(RequestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName), ContainerName = tostring(Container.name), SC
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:create @objectRef.resource:pods (@user.username:system\:serviceaccount\:fission* OR @requestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName:*) (@requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation:true OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.capabilities.add:(SYS_ADMIN OR NET_ADMIN OR SYS_PTRACE))
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb=create objectRef.resource=pods
| spath output=fissionEnv path=requestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName
| spath output=fissionUid path=requestObject.metadata.labels{}
| search (user.username="system:serviceaccount:fission*" OR fissionEnv=*)
| spath output=priv path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.privileged
| spath output=ape path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
| spath output=caps path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.capabilities.add{}
| where priv="true" OR ape="true" OR match(caps,"SYS_ADMIN|NET_ADMIN|SYS_PTRACE")
| table _time user.username objectRef.namespace requestObject.metadata.generateName fissionEnv priv ape caps
| sort - _time

Inside the inbox: Why cybercriminals want to break into your email account

ESET WeLiveSecurity
2026-06-29 4 use cases 3 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

Your inbox is an identity system all of its own: whoever owns it may own a lot more

ATT&CKT1190 T1566 T1566.001
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
—
Phase 2
Weaponization
—
Phase 3
Delivery
Detected

Exploitation
Detected
Phase 5
Installation
Likely
Phase 6
Command & Control
Likely
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-48558 — SimpleHelp Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-29 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

SimpleHelp contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the OIDC authentication flow. When OIDC authentication is configured, identity tokens submitted during login are accepted without verifying their cryptographic signature. In a vulnerable configuration, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can submit a forged token containing arbitrary identity claims to obtain a fully authenticated technician session. In some configurations, this may also allow bypass of multi-factor authentication. Vendor: SimpleHelp , Product: SimpleHelp. Federal patch due: 2026-07-02.

Hunts inbound HTTP requests whose path uses the 'dashboard..' / 'dashboard%2e%2e' / 'dashboard..%2f' prefix-confusion token that escapes the admin-dist root in Nezha's NoRoute fallback handler. This is the exact unauthenticated file-read primitive of CVE-2026-53519 (fixed in 2.0.13) used to reach data/config.yaml and data/sqlite.db. Rationale: The token 'dashboard' immediately followed by '..'/'%2e%2e'/'..%2f' (no separating slash) is the exact bypass string from the advisory PoC and has no benign form — legitimate asset requests are always '/dashboard/'. Cross-checked NVD (CVSS 9.1, fixed 2.0.13) and public PoC. ImWebSession chosen for ASIM portability; W3CIISLog (csUriStem+csUriQuery) or CommonSecurityLog (RequestURL) work identically if the tenant proxies via IIS/WAF instead. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53519 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5c25-7vpj-9mqh • https://github.com/tar-xz/CVE-2026-53519-PoC
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Tenable/Qualys) firing the CVE-2026-53519 template against internal Nezha instances
  • Internal red-team or pentest validating the patch on 2.0.13
  • Security researcher replaying the PoC in a lab that ships logs to the same SIEM
  • A WAF that URL-decodes and re-logs the request, producing a duplicate 'dashboard..' event per hit
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0") // add authorized scanner/pentest source IPs here to suppress sanctioned CVE-2026-53519 template runs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full request path and HTTP status for the source IP; a 200 with Content-Type application/yaml or a sqlite body means the secret was served (pivot to UC2). Check the Nezha version banner — anything <2.0.13 is vulnerable. 2) CONTAIN: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, take the Nezha dashboard off the public internet, and immediately rotate jwt_secret_key AND agent_secret_key in data/config.yaml (invalidates any forged admin JWT), then force-logout all sessions. 3) HUNT: search the same source IP for follow-on '/dashboard../data/sqlite.db' reads and for anomalous admin logins/API-token use after the request time; upgrade to 2.0.13+.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url contains "/dashboard.." or Url contains "/dashboard%2e" or Url contains "dashboard..%2f" or Url contains "dashboard%2e%2e"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nezha WebSocket terminal/file-manager session hijack — one stream UUID attached from 2+ source IPs AIExploitation High
Hunts the GHSA-q6xx-5vr8-p898 cross-tenant RCE: the same live /ws/terminal/<uuid> or /ws/file/<uuid> stream UUID is attached to from two or more distinct client IPs. Legitimately exactly one client (the creator) connects per stream UUID, so a second concurrent attach on a live UUID is the hijack itself. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoints /ws/terminal/:id and /ws/file/:id and the invariant that createTerminal returns one UUID to one client, so >1 distinct attaching source IP on a single UUID is high-fidelity for the hijack. Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because the discriminating field (the UUID in the WebSocket URL path) lives only in reverse-proxy HTTP logs, which EDR/endpoint/cloud-audit telemetry does not carry. Cross-checked against: • https://dailycve.com/nezha-monitoring-websocket-session-hijacking-cross-tenant-rce-ghsa-q6xx-5vr8-p898-critical-dc-jun2026-727/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nezhahq/nezha/CVE-2026-47124/ • https://github.com/nezhahq/nezha
ATT&CKT1190 T1563
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Single user roaming mid-session (laptop→phone, VPN/Wi-Fi flip) so one live UUID legitimately sees two source IPs.
  • Dashboard client opening dual-stack connections logged as separate IPv4 and IPv6 client addresses for the same session.
  • Reverse proxy behind Cloudflare/LB not forwarding X-Forwarded-For — real client IP collapses to edge IP (causes false negatives) or NAT makes two users share one IP.
  • Link-preview / error-reporter bots (Slack unfurl, Sentry) fetching the WebSocket URL harvested from a Referer/breadcrumb — benign but non-owner attach.
  • Uptime/synthetic monitor replaying a captured session URL.
Suppression filter
| extend DistinctSubnets = array_length(set_difference(Clients, dynamic([]))) | extend NetSet = set_difference(zip(Clients), dynamic([])) | where DistinctClients > 1 and not (Endpoint == "" ) // narrow to cross-subnet: replace with dcount over strcat(split(SrcIpAddr,'.')[0..2]) computed in summarize to drop same-/24 roaming and dual-stack pairs
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull every request for the flagged StreamId, order by time; the first source IP is the creator, later IP(s) are suspect. Correlate each source IP's dashboard session (proxy auth cookie / SigninLogs) to a user and confirm the second IP is a different principal, not the owner's dual-stack/VPN address. 2) Contain: If a distinct principal, terminate the live session (kill the ws / restart dashboard), treat the target server as compromised — rotate its SSH keys and credentials (terminal = full shell) — disable the suspected RoleMember, and upgrade Nezha to ≥ v2.0.10. 3) Hunt: Sweep that source IP for other /ws/terminal//ws/file/ UUIDs it touched, inspect the target host for post-exploit artifacts (files written via /ws/file/, new cron, reverse shells), and audit who can read the reverse-proxy logs / Sentry breadcrumbs where UUIDs leak.
let lookback = 3d;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url has "/ws/terminal/" or Url has "/ws/file/"
| extend StreamId = extract(@"/ws/(?:terminal|file)/([0-9a-fA-F\-]{16,})", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(StreamId)
| extend Endpoint = extract(@"/ws/(terminal|file)/", 1, Url)
| summarize DistinctClients = dcount(SrcIpAddr), Clients = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 20), Users = make_set(SrcUsername, 20), Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by StreamId, Endpoint
| where DistinctClients > 1   // exactly one legitimate client attaches per stream UUID; 2+ distinct source IPs on one live UUID = cross-tenant hijack
| order by LastSeen desc

Nezha harvested stream-UUID replay — one client attaching to many distinct terminal/file WebSocket UUIDs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the leaked-UUID abuse path in GHSA-q6xx-5vr8-p898: an attacker who scraped stream UUIDs from proxy logs / Referer / Sentry breadcrumbs replays them, causing one source IP (or account) to attach to an abnormally high number of distinct /ws/terminal/ or /ws/file/ UUIDs in a short window. Rationale: Targets a different pivot than UC1 (fan-out by one client across many UUIDs vs. one UUID across many clients), matching the article's note that attackers passively harvest UUIDs from side channels then replay them. Threshold of >5 distinct UUIDs/hour separates a UUID sweep from a normal operator opening a single session. Non-web telemetry left empty for the same reason as UC1 — the UUID only exists in the reverse-proxy URL path. Cross-checked against: • https://dailycve.com/nezha-monitoring-websocket-session-hijacking-cross-tenant-rce-ghsa-q6xx-5vr8-p898-critical-dc-jun2026-727/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nezhahq/nezha/CVE-2026-47120/
ATT&CKT1078 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate RoleAdmin/operator managing many servers who opens terminals/file managers across the fleet in one session.
  • Automated provisioning or bulk-maintenance tooling that opens file-manager sessions to many hosts from one jump box IP.
  • Shared NAT/VPN egress collapsing several distinct operators to a single source IP, inflating per-IP UUID counts.
  • A single long troubleshooting session that reconnects repeatedly, generating multiple UUIDs from one client.
  • Load balancer or WAF re-issuing requests so the same logical session appears as several UUID hits.
Suppression filter
| where SrcUsername !in~ ("") and DistinctStreams > 5 and SrcUsername !has "admin"  // optional: exclude known fleet-admin service accounts once their normal per-hour session baseline is established
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether the high-fan-out SrcIpAddr/SrcUsername maps to a known admin/operator with legitimate multi-server duties; if unknown or a RoleMember, treat as suspicious. Check whether the UUIDs it hit were created by other users (cross-tenant) vs. its own. 2) Contain: If cross-tenant replay is confirmed, disable the account, block the source IP at the proxy, terminate active sessions, and upgrade Nezha to ≥ v2.0.10 to enforce IsStreamAuthorizedForUser. 3) Hunt: Pivot each hijacked UUID into UC1 to find the true owner and target servers, review those hosts for shell/file-write abuse, and identify the leak channel (proxy log access, Sentry/Bugsnag breadcrumbs, Referer) that exposed the UUIDs.
let lookback = 1d;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url has "/ws/terminal/" or Url has "/ws/file/"
| extend StreamId = extract(@"/ws/(?:terminal|file)/([0-9a-fA-F\-]{16,})", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(StreamId)
| summarize DistinctStreams = dcount(StreamId), Streams = make_set(StreamId, 50), Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctStreams > 5   // one client hitting >5 distinct terminal/file stream UUIDs in an hour indicates replay of harvested UUIDs, not normal single-session use
| order by DistinctStreams desc
